Bui Quang Tuan 2

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: Slide P or move the triangle's corners to build a ring of six circles that closes back on itself.
How to play: Drag a point with a mouse or finger, or focus it and use the arrow keys. Press Check the claim to see what is true here, and use the buttons to show names or the special point.
Look for the math

Bui Quang Tuan found a playful way to place six circles in a triangle: start with one circle in a corner, and let each circle decide where the next one touches a side. The chain comes back to where it started, and a hidden point in the triangle explains how the circles are related.

Six circles that close

P is the centre of C1 and sits on the bisector of angle A1, so C1 touches both sides of that corner. Mark where it touches side A1A2: call that T12. The next circle, C2, touches the very same point while also fitting into corner A2. Its touch point on A2A3 is T23, and C3 fits into corner A3. Continuing gives C4, C5, C6 and then C7 — which lands exactly on C1 again. The logic test checks C7 = C1 on every layout it tries, including all the ways you can drag P.

The touch points share a circle

The six points T12, T23, T34, T45, T56 and T61 are not scattered at random. They all lie on one circle whose centre is the incenter I of the triangle — the centre of its incircle. The dashed green circle in the Gergonne view is the circle through those touch points; the solid blue one is the incircle. They are different circles unless P is chosen just right. The test checks the equal distances on more than 200 triangles.

The point where three lines meet

Let M1, M2 and M3 be the places where the incircle touches the sides opposite A1, A2 and A3. The lines A1M1, A2M2 and A3M3 always meet at one point: the Gergonne point Ge. Each of those lines is also a radical axis of two circles in the chain, so Ge is the radical centre of C2, C4 and C6. And here is the second theorem: if circles C1, C3 and C5 pass through a common point, that point must be Ge; the same goes for C2, C4 and C6.

The word if matters. At the starting P the two triples do not share a point — their radical centres are Ge, but Ge lies outside the circles. Slide P towards the corner A1 and C1, C3, C5 pass through Ge together; slide it away towards the far end of the bisector and C2, C4, C6 do. The logic test finds both positions by bisection and checks that the common point is Ge, then repeats on other triangles. The Java applet's highlight buttons are labelled for the two alternating triples, although its own colour test actually highlights the pairs of circles in one corner (C1 with C4, or C2 with C5); this page follows the labels and the theorem.

What changed from the first theorem

The earlier applet, Six Circles Theorem (Bui Quang Tuan), shows the same ring of six circles and the concyclic touch points. This second applet keeps that picture and adds P, a handle that lets you choose the first circle instead of fixing it, plus the Gergonne construction and the two triples. That is what makes it a different theorem: the circle through the touch points, the incircle and the Gergonne point become visible together.

Try pressing Show Gergonne point, then slide P slowly and watch the dashed cevians keep meeting at the same little dot.
